I have the honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 from a number of people in Alberta communities, including Grande Prairie, Valleyview, Spirit River and Wembley.
These petitioners are concerned that the federal Government's White Paper on Taxation includes tax reform that would still permit 60,000 profitable corporations to pay no income tax at all and they draw to the attention of Parliament that the federal Government is still planning to levy a tax on food and other essential items through a national sales tax and is also failing to provide full indexation to the personal tax system.
Therefore, they call upon the Government of Canada to reject these proposals and especially reject a tax on food. They are asking consideration for the restoration of full indexation to the personal tax system.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION PROHIBITING DISCRIMINATION ON BASIS OF SEXUAL ORIENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a certified petition from a number of Canadian citizens in a number of locations across Canada pointing out that in February, 1985, the Government ordered the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs to prepare a report on equality rights in Canada. In October of that year, the subcommittee on equality rights submitted a report to the House recommending that the Canadian Human Rights Act be amended to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in all areas under federal jurisdiction, including the RCMP and Canadian Armed Forces and in age of consent legislation.
In March, 1986, the Government accepted this report and its recommendations, saying it would take whatever measures are necessary to ensure that sexual orientation is a prohibited ground of discrimination. The Government has yet to introduce significant legislation acting upon these recommendations supported by the Government.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that Government and Parliament act to implement the recommendations contained in the report.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of tabling a large number of petitions from the riding of Saint-Leonard-Anjou, from Western Quebec, Ontario, the South Shore and Vancouver, totalling several hundred signatures.
Your petitioners humbly inform the House that Canada Post's new corporate plan has created two classes of citizens by installing its super boxes in urban and rural areas; that closing rural post offices deprives Canadians of a unique federal presence and reduces postal services that are vital to rural areas; and that rate increases, especially for second class mail, jeopardize the distribution by mail of many newspapers, weeklies, regional papers, magazines and religious publications.
Wherefore your petitioners humbly pray that Parliament reject Canada Post's plan and urge the Corporation to deliver the mail to all Canadian taxpayers, without exception.

subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have a petition from a number of people in Metropolitan Toronto who are concerned that Bill C-55 threatens Canada's traditional commitment to assisting refugees and sets out measures designed to keep most refugee claimants out of the country as opposed to ensuring that genuine refugee claimants are given protection.
Therefore, the petitioners call upon Parliament to ensure that Government and Parliament will withdraw Bill C-55 and substitute legislation embodying the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of the claims of refugee claimants before a refugee board, independent of the immigration commission, universal access to these hearings for every applicant in Canada and the right to appeal on the basis of fact. In duty bound your petitioners will ever pray.

subsubtopic: CANADA POST-OPPOSITION TO REDUCTION IN SERVICE TO RURAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition to the House of Commons and Parliament assembled. The undersigned residents of Canada, at Wilno, Ontario, now avail themselves of their ancient and undoubted right thus to present a grievance common to your petitioners in the certain assurance that your House will therefore provide a remedy, and relevantly declares that the Canada Post Corporation has already started reducing services in certain rural areas of Canada.
The Canada Post Corporation intends to continue systematically to close an important number of post offices in small municipalities. The population is firmly opposed to any reduction in the postal personnel and the normal services to which the rural citizens are entitled. The population does not accept and will not accept at any time that the small communities be penalized by the planned reductions.
For those reasons they ask Parliament to give an immediate answer to their request regarding the fact that their rural communities will not have to suffer any form of discrimination to the quality of their postal services. They ask that Parliament agree that the rural municipalities will not be penalized by the closing of their post offices.
They finally ask that the rural communities which have already been badly affected by the reductions will recover the complete postal services to which they were accustomed. The fight for the Wilno post office is the fight of every rural community in Canada. They want to retain those services.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to again address this House to encourage the passage of Bill C-75 at second reading. It deals with the implementation of the agreement between the Governments of Canada and Nova Scotia on offshore petroleum resource management and revenue sharing.
Moreover, this Bill contains certain measures from previous agreements which were retained and modified to make them consistent with the new agreement.
As this second reading will broaden the debate, it seems to me normal that the Minister responsible for this sector, who I
Canada-Nova Scotia Accord
am representing today, should put forward the necessary information as a representative of the Government of Canada. The Minister together with his provincial counterpart will be responsible for enforcing the application of the Act which is under his responsibility.
I wish to discuss briefly the heart of the Bill. The passage of this Bill, which was tabled before the House for first reading on June 26, 1987, will enable the Government of Canada to respect its commitment to the Government of Nova Scotia whose corresponding provincial Act was passed on May 19, 1987. In fact, this legislation is mirror legislation to that passed by the Nova Scotia provincial Government on May 29, 1987. It will show the manifest solidarity of the Government of Canada with the Government of Nova Scotia in terms of the importance that we attach to the legislative framework within which resource exploitation will take place.
The accord which we seek to ratify today will replace the Canada-Nova Scotia Agreement of 1982 on offshore petroleum and gas resource management and revenue sharing. This new accord contains several improvements, which I will discuss later in detail.
If I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, I will cite a few now. First, it will ratify the creation of an independent body to administer and regulate all aspects of offshore petroleum and gas activities. Second, it will modify the development fund so that $200 million will no longer be considered as a loan, but will now be considered as a grant. Third, it will authorize the payment of the sum of $25 million by the Government of Canada to Nova Scotia Resources Ltd. which will enable it to participate in the exploitation and development of offshore activities.
This agreement, which is intended to build on the Atlantic Accord, will give concrete form to a co-management concept which both levels of Government wish to make effective and efficient. Furthermore, it will be consistent with this Government's over-all approach to the management of eastern Canada's offshore resources.
When the Prime Minister, (Mr. Mulroney), signed the agreement on August 26, 1986, he correctly observed that, "This accord constitutes a clear improvement over the 1982 agreement, in that it makes Nova Scotia a full partner in the development of its offshore area".
As you can see once again, Mr. Speaker, the era of confrontation with the provinces, fueled in the past by the previous Government, is well and truly over. Only through co-operation, actively encouraged by this Government since September, 1984, will we build a strong and united Canada. The fundamental option that we took as a Government at that time means that today we can reap the fruit of our efforts, and make them work, not only for Nova Scotia but for Canada as a whole.

becomes ..." Therefore, we have not dragged our feet in energy matters; we have helped to bring harmony to a country that had been previously divided. One only has to be reminded of the national energy policy perpetrated on the country by the previous administration to understand what we mean when we talk about division.
I wish to discuss briefly the objectives of the agreement. The Governments of Canada and Nova Scotia have therefore agreed, through this accord, that the petroleum and gas resources of the offshore area must be developed in such a way as to harmonize the interests of all Canadians, particularly those in Nova Scotia, and that a durable and profitable socioeconomic infrastructure is essential.
The agreement is designed to establish a fair tax system and consistent administration of the petroleum resources which are based on the same principle of equity and parity that prevail with the other producing provinces, taking into account the special situation of the offshore area.
The sanction by Parliament of this Bill will endorse the development of the petroleum resources at the earliest opportunity, in the interest of both Governments, and will thus contribute to the security of our energy supplies. It will also confirm Nova Scotia as the principal beneficiary of the activities related to the petroleum resources, and will enable its Government, among other things, to see the benefit of the measures adopted, as if the resources were on land.
Finally, it will reaffirm the equality of the two levels of Government with respect to the actual management of the resources and the maximization of the economic and industrial benefits for Canada and Nova Scotia.
1 wish to discuss the key elements of the agreement. The Bill that we are proposing today takes into account the Canada Petroleum Resources Act, which deals with the management of petroleum rights, and which we passed earlier this year, as well as the Canada Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act, which deals with the technical regulation of offshore petroleum activities.
As the provisions of the Crown share contained in the 1982 agreement with Nova Scotia were repealed in 1985, we negotiated with the provincial Government a new arrangement which makes it eligible to receive from the Government of Canada annual payments equal to the share of net profits that it would have received under the previous arrangement with respect to offshore projects. This measure should reflect more accurately the actual costs and revenues of the projects in question. It will remain in effect until Nova Scotia reaches the average of the tax level of the other Canadian provinces.
The result is that the Nova Scotia Government is given the responsibility for setting and collecting royalties, as if those resources were on its territory and, therefore, administering the revenues from petroleum and gas activities. The provisions on equalization contained in the 1982 agreement are maintained in this agreement.
I should like to explain briefly the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore petroleum board for my colleagues. The actual concept of co-management will take on its full meaning in the creation of an independent body which will replace the present Canada-Nova Scotia Petroleum and Gas Resources Board. The mandate of the new board will be to make decisions on matters directly affecting the management of offshore petroleum resources. The offices and personnel of the board will be in Nova Scotia and will perform the functions previously performed by the Canadian Oil and Gas Lands Administration with regard to all offshore operations in Nova Scotia.
The body in question will be called the Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Petroleum Board and will be composed of five members including a chairman appointed by both Governments. The latter will appoint two members respectively and may appoint alternate members to act as members of the board in the absence or incapacity of any of the regular members. Furthermore, not more than two members of the board may be public servants of the signing Governments.
The board will make decisions on announcing discoveries. It will regulate activities in the petroleum fields and exercise special powers in emergencies. It will also approve the technical aspects of development plans. It will collect royalties. It will carry out public inquiries designed to elucidate matters related to its mandate. It will make recommendations in respect of possible amendments to the Act or regulations flowing from the agreement.
Certain decisions of the board considered vital will require the ratification of both Governments. Examples would be the call for tenders, the ensuing issuance of exploration permits, the definition of specifications related to major discoveries and to production licences, as well as the final approval of development plans. As the decision related to certain Nova Scotia projects is specified in the Bill, they will require only the approval of the provincial counterpart, the Minister responsible for energy in Nova Scotia.
Like other producing provinces, Nova Scotia may now, as a result of the passage of this Bill, participate fully in the negotiations and consultations with the Government of Canada in all matters related to offshore petroleum.
The 1982 agreement saw the creation of a development fund of $200 million to put in place the necessary infrastructure, but before any petroleum and gas production would begin. In the new accord the Government of Canada renounces that condition.
I will now refer to the drilling fund. We had agreed, within the framework of the drilling fund created with a view to bringing offshore petroleum rapidly into production, to pay a sum of $25 million to Nova Scotia Resources Ltd. so that it could participate in the exploration and bringing into production of petroleum in the offshore area of Nova Scotia.
October 29, 1987

We included in this Act the provisions related to environmental protection contained in the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act which guarantee the same protection for all other frontier lands. In the event of an offshore disaster, the future Act provides for a financial compensation plan for fishermen, or other persons affected, for any damage resulting from wastes or spills.
Subject to ministerial directives, the board will determine the need for a public review in relation to the exercise of any of its powers or the performance of any of its duties when such a review proves necessary. The board may establish terms of reference in a timetable which will permit a comprehensive review of all aspects of the matter and appoint the commissioner or commissioners.
It may require the person who proposed the potential development to submit a preliminary development plan, an environmental impact statement, a socio-economic impact statement, as well as a benefits plan. Finally, it may require that the commissioner or commissioners hold public hearings in the province or elsewhere in Canada and report on them to itself as well as to both Governments.
I should like to make a brief statement on access to production. Aware of the need to reduce substantially Nova Scotia's dependence on foreign oil, the two Governments agreed to encourage within that province the use of oil and gas produced off the East Coast. Furthermore, in the event of a shortage of petroleum in the province, when deliveries are insufficient, Nova Scotia will be given first choice in purchasing under market conditions offshore petroleum not included in a contract.
I should also like to allude to some of the benefits. I see that both parties finally agree to ensure the maximum of the benefits related to offshore petroleum activity for all Canadians, particularly for Nova Scotians. The benefits plan submitted to the board by companies fully involved in offshore exploration must indicate that first consideration will be given to competitive goods and services produced in Nova Scotia and, consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, that workers in that province will be given first consideration for training and employment.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think you can see that the passage of the Act will mark another milestone in the history of the country, the now more harmonious history, I might add, of federal-provincial relations. The Act will finally sanction the regional development to which Nova Scotia is entitled that in turn will result in the creation of new jobs. The economic and industrial benefits are significant for both Nova Scotia and indeed for Canada.
Although Martin Heidegger maintained that "the will to do something is tantamount to accomplishing it,"-and that is from page 102 of Essays and Lectures by Gallimard-it seems to me that we must take one more step in the right direction by ratifying as quickly as possible this important accord, because
Canada-Nova Scotia Accord
the Government and the people of Nova Scotia are awaiting its passage.

subtopic: CANADA-NOVA SCOTIA OFFSHORE PETROLEUM RESOURCES ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to speak on this piece of legislation, Bill C-75. I find this to be rather perplexing in that we are dealing today with a piece of legislation which is completely irrelevant at the present time because of the policies of this Government toward the offshore, particularly the offshore off the East Coast of Canada.
The short title of the Bill we are debating today is the "Canada-Nova Scotia Offshore Petroleum Resources Accord Implementation Act". Not only is the Government's policy completely incomprehensive, it practically made the short title of the Bill incomprehensive.
I am very concerned about quite a few things in respect of the offshore and the Government's policy. First, I would like to deal with the way the Government has tried to frustrate the implementation of energy policy in the country. In January there was an Energy Ministers' conference, which was to be the way that energy policy would be formulated. The energy Ministers of the ten provinces and the federal Minister of Energy met, and they were to meet again during the summer to formulate the ideas which the various public servants and bureaucrats of the respective provinces had formulated during the intervening period.
They met in January. Of course, there were the discussions, all the talk and the completely ridiculous statements the Energy Ministers made about how they would solve the energy policy problems of Canada. To begin with, the federal Minister of Energy did not even wait for the summer and a second meeting of energy Ministers to say what he wanted to do. In June he came out with a paper entitled Energy Security in Canada which does not deal with the question of security of supply at all. In fact, the main thrust of this publication by the Minister is to stockpile oil in case there is a shortage of it in Canada, but I will get into that later.
First, we have the Minister instigating a meeting of Energy Ministers. He did not wait to meet a second time before coming out with his own policy. When the second meeting took place in St. John's in August it fell flatter than a pancake. Then we have the second attempt in the spring of 1987 before the first attempt was completed. The second attempt was "Energy Options" and a well known individual on Bay Street, Mr. Thomas Kierans, was asked to head a committee and make recommendations for energy policy. If you want to get someone to determine energy policy in Canada, Bay Street is not the best place to go. Nevertheless, this is what the Minister of Energy did.
There was a meeting in Calgary in June and since then there have been other meetings. The hearings will be wound up in Montreal in December. We do not know what will be brought

October 29, 1987
Canada-Nova Scotia Accord
forward, but that did not stop the Government with respect to the Energy Ministers.
A third link was started. The Government brought forward the recommendations of the White Paper on Tax Reform which are completely contrary to developing energy security. The Government when it was in Opposition said that there should not be grandiose energy programs in Canada, such as the Petroleum Incentive Program, that they are too costly and there are better ways of developing energy reserves and encouraging some energy security in Canada.
The present Government said in the 1984 election campaign that it would do it through the tax system. But what did the Government do? It came out with a White Paper and cut back tax programs to encourage the development of oil and gas. While it knows it is cutting back the incentives to develop oil and gas projects in Canada, the Government feels the projects should be encouraged through special programs targeted to those particular or respective energy projects. The Government has reversed itself completely.
In 1984 during the election campaign the Conservatives said that oil and gas development should be encouraged through the tax system, yet in this year's White Paper the Government said no, that it wanted to cut back the assistance through the tax system to target various projects. Not only did this break the promise in the election campaign about help through the tax system, it changed the Government's position completely about not targeting for special projects.

subtopic: CANADA-NOVA SCOTIA OFFSHORE PETROLEUM RESOURCES ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: You are grasping at straws.

subtopic: CANADA-NOVA SCOTIA OFFSHORE PETROLEUM RESOURCES ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Now the Government is saying that it is going to target special projects. But we really do not know what the Government means because the Government has not done anything constructive to date. What is the Government doing through the White Paper? First, it has cut back on the put in use rule which was very important in Canada because it was targeted largely to major projects. The put in use rule said that you cannot use deductions for major projects until they are actually put in use.
If you have an offshore project, perhaps a Hibernia, where a gravity based drilling operation is to be put in place costing between four and five billion dollars, the developers, Mr. Speaker, cannot use deductions until the platform is actually put in use, costing the developers millions of dollars.
The Government said that the rule would apply to property acquired after 1989 and stipulated that neither the capital cost allowance nor the income tax credits could be used prior to an asset being put in use or, if earlier, the year in which the construction of the asset is completed.
In addition to the put-in use stipulation, the Government cut the rate of capital cost allowance for these types of projects in drilling and exploration facilities from 30 per cent to 25 per cent.
Third, in the White Paper, with respect to the investment tax credit, the Government did not touch the actual rate of 25 per cent for high cost exploration. That is unchanged, but the Government proposed that the investment tax credit could only be applied to one-half of the federal tax payable.
With these three stipulations, the Government of Canada has greatly reduced the inclination of possible developers from going to the East Coast and developing oil and gas reserves existing in that area. That applies not only to the East Coast but to the Beaufort as well. That was the third attempt at trying to set some energy policy.
Fourth, the most recent one, is the free trade agreement. It completely nullifies and makes obsolete the other ideas which the Government said it would bring forward, not that those ideas were ever going to come forward. We have only the Government's word that there would be any ideas coming forward. I would like to deal with the free trade agreement later on, but I want now to concentrate on the offshore.
We have a tremendously serious situation because of lack of activity. I want to refer to some things said by the Parliamentary Secretary. He said that things are wonderful now because there is no confrontation with the provinces. We are talking about an agreement between Canada and Nova Scotia which replaces an agreement entered into between Nova Scotia and the previous Liberal Government. Not only that, the agreement between Nova Scotia and the former Liberal Government was entered into in the final days before the election in 1984. Nova Scotia obviously wanted to enter into that agreement. There was no confrontation or bad feeling between Canada and Nova Scotia at that point. In fact, the way it looks right now Nova Scotia would have done better by sticking with that agreement than entering into this second one with the present Government.
We criticize the Crown's share and say that the Crown's shares are no longer applicable. The present agreement says that Nova Scotia will get something, but the federal Government is doing absolutely nothing to promote the offshore. Until the federal Government does something to promote the offshore, to create some activity, there will be no activity, and Nova Scotia will reap none of the benefits from the production of oil and gas. What the Government has been saying about the relations between the Province of Nova Scotia and former Liberal Governments is just not true. In fact, those relations were most cordial.
This Bill will do to develop oil and gas on the offshore. There is nothing here. It is only a means of conducting meetings and of regulating what will happen if perchance exploration and development does take place, but it is not taking place. Until actual exploration is carried out in Nova Scotia and there is development of the oil and gas reserves, this Bill will just be an academic exercise.
October 29, 1987

The Parliamentary Secretary said as well that this Bill will cut Nova Scotia's dependence on foreign oil. That is just not true. This Bill will not do anything to cut Nova Scotia's dependence on foreign oil. For instance, at the present time we in Atlantic Canada are dependent almost exclusively on imported oil. In fact, in 1986 the whole of Atlantic Canada relied on foreign oil for 99 per cent of the oil that was used. The Province of Quebec relied on foreign oil for 60 per cent of the oil it used in 1986.
In Atlantic Canada, 180,000 barrels of foreign oil a day were imported in 1986. In the first nine months of 1987, that increased from 180,000 barrels per day to 200,000 barrels per day. The actual dependence on foreign oil is increasing.
We have the reserves but nothing is being done to develop them. The one puny utterance from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) was contained in this document, Energy Security in Canada, in which he advocates stockpiling oil. He does not advocate moving ahead to develop the reserves that exist in the offshore. He wants to stockpile foreign oil. That is fine as an interim solution, but that is no plan for developing the energy security of this country.
The Parliamentary Secretary said that this Bill gives Nova Scotians, in times of shortages of supply, the ability to have the first option on oil produced in Nova Scotia. I would like to refer to Clause 39 of the Bill which is entitled "Regional Security of Supply." Clause 39(2) reads:
(2) Where there is a shortfall of petroleum deliveries in the Province, the Provincial Minister may, after consulting with the Federal Minister, give notice to holders of production licences in the offshore area that the consumers and facilities referred to in paragraphs (l)(a), (b) and (c) that are specified in the notice have, during the term of the notice, the First option to acquire, on commercial terms, petroleum produced in the offshore area unless a sales contract with respect to that petroleum has been entered into prior to the giving of the notice.
For one thing, of course, it is dependent upon a sales contract not having been entered into. That, of course, is a very big "if'. Second, it flies in the face of the Government's free trade agreement with the United States. The Government cannot now make assurances to Nova Scotia or to any other province that it will get this kind of priority access to its own reserves. The Government saw to that. It gave away any right that Nova Scotia or any province would have to the first option to production in its jurisdiction. We do not know where that oil will go or where the natural gas will go. The free trade agreement makes sure of that.
I would certainly agree that the Parliamentary Secretary stated the philosophy of his Government when he said the will to do something is tantamount to accomplishing it. The will is the only thing it has, because it has not accomplished anything in developing the offshore of this country. If the will exists, it is certainly a well-kept secret.
This summer we were supposed to have, according to the statements of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), some agreement with the developers and the owners of Hibernia. We did not get anything. The Minister of Transport said, as
Canada-Nova Scotia Accord
reported by his local newspaper, that they are asking too much, they are not being fair. This coming from the same Government that says we should let the private sector develop our energy opportunities. This is the same Government that says we should let Petro-Canada operate as a private sector corporation and not restrict it to being an arm of public policy. Yet at the same time, it will blame the lead players in the development of Hibernia for not doing anything.
We do not know what this Government is doing. We certainly have not heard anything from it as to what it will be doing to try to help develop the oil and gas reserves off the East Coast of Canada.
It is completely ridiculous that the Government would say that it is doing something to develop these reserves. Just recently, when he was in St. John's, the Minister of Energy told the people of Newfoundland that the free trade agreement would be good for the development of Hibernia. He said that with the free trade agreement, Hibernia will have all sorts of new markets. Atlantic Canada is 99 per cent dependent on foreign oil. Quebec is 60 per cent dependent on foreign oil. What is wrong with the markets that already exist?
Is the Minister saying that the oil and gas off the East Coast of Canada is not good enough for Atlantic Canadians and the people of Quebec, that it should not be wasted there but should really be sold in the United States if it is to have any major purpose whatsoever? That is just ludicrous and it is an insult to the people of eastern Canada.
We have been told that under the free trade agreement, even in times of energy shortages, the United States is to get a proportionate amount of Canada's energy. That is quite significant, particularly with respect to oil. This country is rapidly running out of supplies of light and medium crude. It is not the policy of the Liberal Party to say that we should not be selling oil to the United States. Up until the free trade agreement, we had the National Energy Board to tell us when we would be running short and when we would have a scarcity of supply. We relied on it to do this job.
The Liberal Party was the first Party to endorse the decision of the National Energy Board to do away with the surplus test. We felt that that was the best way to go. It was fair to the suppliers of natural gas and it was in the best interests not only of the sale of Canadian natural gas to the United States but to the development of new reserves.
We did not and could not, nor could anybody, accept the Conservative Government's agreement to completely gut the National Energy Board. We will not know when we are running short and, if we do, we will not be able do anything about it.
We have said that we will give a proportionate amount of our energy to the United States and we do not know how much that will be. Let us just look at some of the rumours we have been hearing about energy. Supposedly there will be a block period which will indicate what percentage will be going to the

October 29, 1987
Canada-Nova Scotia Accord
United States. We do not know when that block period will be, or for how long it will be, but supposedly that is what it will be. If that block period is the first six months of 1987, then 37 per cent of all oil produced in Canada will be earmarked for the United States, because in the first six months of 1987, 37 per cent of all the oil produced in Canada was sold to the United States. That means we are obligated even at times when we do not have security of supply for our own needs.
The Government is backing away from developing an energy policy, which means we do not have the assurance that our supplies of light and medium crude are going to be replaced through new projects, such as oil and gas on the East Coast, the tar sands, the Beaufort, or through upgrading. We do not have that assurance because the Government has waffled for three years on this question. We are no further ahead now than we were in September of 1984, regardless of all the government statements, commissions, committees, brochures, periodicals, and free trade agreements with the U.S.
The Atlantic Accord did nothing to help the oil and gas industry off the coast of Newfoundland. Now we are talking about the Nova Scotia offshore and this Bill will not make any difference at all. In 1987, this year, only $33 million has been spent on the Nova Scotia offshore. It is only because of the grandfathering of the Petroleum Incentives Program that we have that. That was put in place by the former Government. In 1984, $600 million was spent on the Nova Scotia offshore, so it is completely ludicrous for the Government to say it is concerned about exploration in the Nova Scotia offshore.
Under this agreement the Government turned the $200 million loan under the former agreement into a grant, but look at where the money was spent. Some of it went into things that were not even within miles of the Nova Scotia coastline. That is not easy because it is almost completely surrounded by water. The money was turned into a political slush fund.
What about the $25 million for Nova Scotia Resources Ltd. to develop its reserves in Nova Scotia? That, unfortunately, is woefully inadequate for that company which has a very high debt. Unless it is able to take part in some kind of profitable development of oil or gas very soon, the situation is only going to get worse.
What we want is to develop the reserves to add to the security of supply in Canada, which is minimal at the present. We want the Government to stand by what it said it was going to do-develop security of supply. Do not tell me that the major players in projects like Hibernia and Venture do not want to go ahead. It is up to the Government to develop a fiscal regime that will encourage them to do so. After all, it is the Tory Government that said the private sector was going to do it.
It is no good to say that the Government will give loan guarantees to Mobil. That company does not need loan guarantees. It is not going to go broke. What they want is a
plan. They also want to make money, of course, and the Government said there is nothing wrong with that. If Mobil makes a profit, that is great. However, there is something very important at stake here and that is energy security for Canadians. The Government has to do what it said it was going to do, get development going on the East Coast. This legislation is not going to have any effect at all until the Government develops the political will to do something for Nova Scotia.
A great deal of this legislation is similar to the wording in the Atlantic Accord. There are a few things in there that I question and I will do that in committee, but that is the easy part. The difficult part is to get the Government to realize the importance of the offshore to Nova Scotia as well as Newfoundland, indeed to all of Atlantic Canada, and to start honouring the commitments it made, take them seriously and not just try and slough off this very important industry in Atlantic Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to say a few words on behalf of my Party concerning Bill C-75, which implements the agreement between the Government of Canada and the Government of Nova Scotia dealing with the offshore.
Before I do that, since this is the first time I have had an opportunity to say a few words in my new capacity as energy critic for the NDP, I want to pay tribute to the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). For many years he was a very competent spokesman on energy for our Party. I want to say how much I, my Leader, and all of us in caucus appreciated the contribution he made in this field. He had some expertise in this area gained in the work he did before being elected to this House and made a great contribution, not only on behalf of his Party but on behalf of all Members of Parliament, to understanding the problems of energy in this country. The Hon. Member has done some good work on this particular issue, offshore resource development, made a few speeches and raised a number of questions.
As the House already knows from those speeches and others, our Party of course supports the agreement we have before us today. This is simply mirror legislation to that already passed in the Nova Scotia Legislature a number of weeks ago. The most important thing we can do today is raise some questions about the future of energy in this country and then send it off to committee for detailed study. There we can call in experts and government officials and make sure we scrutinize the Bill very closely.
This Bill is very similar to Bill C-6, an agreement between Canada and the Government of Newfoundland on the Newfoundland offshore. It is very similar as well to the Atlantic Accord which has already been dealt with in this House.
As I said, we support this arrangement but we have a number of questions we want to raise in committee. Those
October 29, 1987

questions will be positive, of course, and I want to say a couple of very positive things about the Bill before us today.
First, I am glad to see that there is an agreement between the Government of Canada and the Government of Nova Scotia. There was a time in the 1970s and early 1980s when this kind of agreement was not possible. I am not going to place the blame for that squarely and solely on the doorstep of the former Government. The 1970s were very turbulent times in the oil business around the world and in Canada. It was very difficult at that time to come to this kind of agreement. It was also a time when a great constitutional debate was taking place and these kinds of agreements were more difficult to achieve.
The second positive aspect about this agreement is that it now includes provincial involvement in the offshore business in Canada. I believe provincial involvement is very important, and I suggest that we should try to carry this a step further and consider a constitutional amendment to enshrine provincial control of offshore resources in the Constitution of Canada. That is very important to provinces like Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
I know how important it is to Saskatchewan for the Constitution of Canada to include some control regarding energy. In 1981 our Party was instrumental in persuading the government of the day to insert in the Constitution of Canada an amendment which provided for some control over resources for provinces like Saskatchewan and Alberta. I believe that was a very important step in terms of our controlling and husbanding resources such as gas and oil and potash which are so important for our development.
I know the importance of this control because in Saskatchewan we have a gas and oil industry and a potash industry. We have many other natural resource industries. Such control is also important to Alberta, and we should seriously consider a constitutional amendment extending the same kinds of rights to people in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia in regard to offshore energy.
I want to raise a number of questions about the Bill which I know have been raised in Nova Scotia, and before in the House. For example, it is not clear whether there is enough protection in the legislation for aboriginal land claims in the Province of Nova Scotia. I suggest the committee should closely examine the Bill to make sure that the rights of aboriginal people, our original Canadian citizens, are adequately protected in Bill C-75. I also want to make sure that there are some public rights to inspect development and benefit plans in the Province of Nova Scotia, and that there is adequate access to information and adequate benefits in terms of royalties to-the Province of Nova Scotia. We must have enough details and information about how these programs regarding royalties and other benefits will be carried out under this legislation.
Canada-Nova Scotia Accord
My third concern is that, according to my understanding of the legislation and the comments I have heard, there is no provision for an independent environmental impact assessment of what this will mean in the offshore of Nova Scotia. There should be provision for an environmental impact study, because the environment is important not only to today's generation, but to the generations of the future.
My fourth concern is that there is no requirement for a public hearing process on applications. This is another question that should be considered at committee stage.
The fifth and probably most important concern of Nova Scotians about this agreement between their government and the Government of Canada is that there may be inadequate protection for the fishery on Georges Bank in relation to offshore drilling. The Georges Bank is one of the richest fishing banks, not only in this country but in the entire world. There is some concern in the Province of Nova Scotia that the Bill should provide more protection for this extremely wealthy renewable resource from offshore drilling.
For example, I am aware that Texaco is attempting to get permission to drill in the Georges Bank. While oil and gas is important to the future of Nova Scotia and this country we must never forget that the fishery is a much wealthier resource, a renewable resource and one that we must protect with all our ability so that it will continue to produce for many generations to come. I understand there was some protection for the fishery on Georges Bank in the previous accord five years ago. Although it may not have been adequate in 1982, that protection has now been removed.
Finally, I believe the committee should ask some serious questions about the protection of security of supply for the people of Nova Scotia. I am not convinced that anything in this legislation addresses the issue of adequate security of supply.
Let me conclude by making some general observations about this legislation. I have not seen from this Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) or his predecessor, the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), any vision or plan for the future of energy policy in this country other than relying on the private sector and primarily the huge American multinational corporations to develop energy for us. I do not see any vision to Canadianize the industry, to control it for Canada, to plan our developments and, in some cases, conserve the gas and oil for future generations.
Rather than a true Canadian plan, I see something that makes me fearful as a Canadian. It is a continental energy policy in the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States that will develop our energy in this country lockstep with the energy needs of the United States of America.
As we debate this legislation before the House today, we must raise questions about the future security of supply for Nova Scotians, Newfoundlanders, Albertans and all Canadians. We must ask how we can use that resource to best develop

October 29, 1987
Canada-Nova Scotia Accord
our country, create jobs, and provide energy supply at a reasonable price for Canadians.
The most serious aspect of the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States is the complete integration of the North American energy market in Canada and the United States. In fact, President Reagan said that this free trade agreement is the economic constitution of North America.
The Hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie), the former mayor of Toronto, is in the House. I know that as mayor of Toronto he wanted substantial control at City Council in order for the people of Toronto to make decisions that affected their own lives.
I argue that the same thing pertains in this situation. Canadians should have the ultimate say on the price of energy in this country, and the ultimate say over security of supply. According to the free trade agreement, the only option available is to charge the same price to Canadian consumers as we charge to consumers to whom we are exporting in the United States.
I was in the House in the 1970s when there was a tremendous increase in the price of oil. Many people supported a two-price system at that time which kept the price for Canadian farmers in my riding, of whom there are thousands, at a much lower price than they would have had to pay if we were to charge our farmers the world price. People were able to heat their homes for a much lower price because we had a two-price system. People were able to pay a lower price for gasoline because we had a two-price system.
If we adopt this free trade agreement we will not be able to adopt such a system, because we will have to charge the same price for the person in Kamsack, Toronto or Halifax as someone in Los Angeles, Chicago or San Francisco. I believe it is detrimental to the future of Canada to give away our sovereignty.
While current situations may warrant similar prices now, we do not know if that will be the situation in the future. However, there may be a time when the Government and Parliament of Canada will have to introduce an act similar to that in the 1970s when consumers were cushioned from the crisis in the Middle East when oil prices went through the ceiling in a matter of months. It is beyond me how the party of Sir John A. Macdonald and John Diefenbaker can forever give up this sovereignty over the price of energy in Canada.

speechtext: Simcoe North.

subtopic: CANADA-NOVA SCOTIA OFFSHORE PETROLEUM RESOURCES ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I remember the anger of the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) a few years ago when certain Albertans came out with a bumper sticker that said, "Let the eastern bastards freeze in the dark". There was a lot of anger in this House. I was angry. As a western Canadian, I thought it was a very unfair comment to make about central Canadians. But it will not be Albertans who will say that in the future. It could be the Americans because they control our energy policy, and I do not agree with that.
We could have long term contracts without giving up our right to set a Canadian price. We could have long term contracts without giving up our right to control supply in a time of crisis. What we are giving away in this particular free trade agreement is the right to security of supply because it says that in the time of crisis the United States must have proportional access to the diminished supply in Canada and we must not discriminate on price. We cannot use energy to develop in a discriminatory fashion the economies in Saskatchewan, Manitoba or Quebec because we must charge the same price in the United States.
I hope that becomes a major issue in the next election campaign. If it is, the Conservative Party will be tossed out on its ear because Canadians want their sovereignty and the right to set their own energy prices and to control their own security of supply. That is exactly what the people of this country want. They were very happy back in the 1970s to have a two-price system. The people in my riding were very happy to have that system and I was very proud to support a two-price system that provided the farmers of Kamsack with a price for their fuel that was much lower than they would have had to pay if the Conservative Party had been in power.
October 29, 1987

I want to campaign across this country for the right of Canadians to set their own price and to control their own security of supply. I am surprised that this kind of policy would come from the Party which fought so hard against free trade with the United States in 1911. The party of Sir John A. Macdonald and John Diefenbaker had a Canadian vision. Canadians want to control their own sovereignty and they want the power to make those decisions.
I will conclude by saying that this will be a long debate because it concerns the future of Canada. It is very surprising to me that my Conservative friends opposite want to give up the right to set our own price and the right to control our security of supply. That is an incredible thing. I ask my friends opposite if they are Members of Parliament of this country of Canada, or are they really Congressmen from the United States, because they are giving those rights to Washington and not to Canada? Our Party will fight them on that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (for the Minister of State (Finance)) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-87, an Act respecting the imposition of duties of customs and other charges to give effect to the international convention on the harmonized commodity description and coding system, to provide relief against the imposition of certain duties of customs or other charges, to provide for other related matters, and to amend or repeal certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure today to introduce Bill C-87 which will replace the existing Customs Tariff and incorporate the provisions of the Duties Relief Act. This is the bulkiest legislative measure ever tabled in the House-three tomes and 1,905 pages.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill reflects the Governmen't pledge to implement the new Customs Tariff by January 1, 1988. Parliament was made aware of the Government's intention through notices of ways and means motions tabled with the
Customs Tariff
Budget documents on February 26, 1986 and February 18,
1987.	The Bill will also enable us to enforce the detailed provisions of the notice of ways and means motion tabled in the House on Friday, October 2, 1987.
Since our customs legislation had to be overhauled, the Government is introducing measures designed to replace the entire Customs Tariff. The original approach of the new legislation will make it possible for the Government to set up a tariff structure which, as we near the turn of the century, is more in keeping with a modern, technology-based economy.
The Bill has been drafted to account for the principles underlying the Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System. This system is the result of an international endeavour aimed at standardizing the tariff classification and the system of statistics pertaining to commercial exchanges among the world's major trading nations.
Under the harmonized system a given good will basically be classified according to its characteristic or nature rather that the use to which it may be put. It will be classified only once to avoid resorting to multiple choices.
The Harmonized System is an entirely new approach to commodity classification. It was developed in consultation with government and private sector experts, in order to allow for present-day technology and the range of products involved in international trade.
Together with its main trading partners, Canada is committed to implementing the new tariff system as of January 1,
1988.	The tabling of this Bill in the House was an important step in a lengthy process that started in 1981, when the Canadian Government decided to adopt the Harmonized System.
In 1981, most countries were using a common commodity classification system for customs purposes. The system, developed in Brussels by the Customs Co-operation Council, was the predecessor of the Harmonized System.
Canada and the United States each had a different system for tariff classification. Both countries understood the advantages of using a system they would share with the rest of the world. That is why we participated in the development of the Harmonized System, together with the other members of the Council, including major trading countries such as the members of the Common Market and Japan.
Canada has an important role to play internationally by helping improve the climate of trading relations, and this Bill will help it play that role. The Harmonized System is an important step towards a more rational and more specific world trading system. Adopting this system will benefit our importers and Canadian business people in general.
The new Customs Tariff is set up in a more logical manner, which makes things easier for the importer and for the customs officers who have to classify imported goods and determine the applicable duty. This should simplify import formalities and

October 29, 1987
Customs Tariff
reduce the number of appeals from tariff classification decisions.
The Elarmonized System also lends itself better to computerized import procedures. Revenue Canada has developed a brand new data processing system that will be introduced at the same time as the Harmonized System. The private sector has also taken steps to adjust its methods for processing imports and exports to the Harmonized System. As of January 1, 1988, importers will face fewer administrative formalities and be able to clear goods through Customs faster then was the case under the old system. The new system will also result in a savings to business and the Government.
As far as international trade negotiations are concerned, by adopting the Harmonized System, countries will be better able to understand their respective tariffs. The outlook for multilateral trade negotiations like the Uruguay Round in which Canada is participating today would be considerably brighter.
The Harmonized System also provides for a statistical coding system integrated in the tariff classification system, which will vastly improve the statistical data on Canada's imports and exports. This process will also make it easier to compare Canada's trading statistics with those of other countries.
The proposed new tariff was adopted only after close public consultation. A working paper highlighting the benefits flowing from the adoption of the new tariff classification system had been released in 1981. In 1984, draft tariff provisions covering all goods included in the current Customs Tariff, converted to the harmonized system, were submitted to the Tariff Board for public consultation. Board officials held public hearings on the Government's proposals and heard evidence from commercial organizations, corporations, consultants and customs brokers. Their testimony and the board's detailed analysis were the basis of recommendations contained in the four reports tabled in the House.
The Bill now before the House features a great many of the Tariff Board's recommendations. It also takes into consideration the results of the international trade negotiations to which Canada was party so that the rights of our trade partners will be respected throughout the conversion process.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) for his helpful co-operation. He did his utmost to keep importers aware of the Customs Tariff amendments we are proposing.
In 1986, Revenue Canada Customs and Excise officials launched a public information program featuring leaflets, briefings and training seminars. This program has been recently accelerated and expanded. Importers and customs brokers from coast to coast were convened to learn more about the impact of the new tariff on their day-to-day activities. They were also able to become familiar with the improved customs processing system scheduled to be set in motion by Revenue Canada on January 1, 1988.
Once the new system is operational, occasionally goods may be classified under an item not provided in the Customs Tariff. The Government will then use a special procedure to deal with any problems that may arise. To enable the Government to respond quickly and efficiently, the draft Bill included a provision that will authorize the Government to make any necessary changes in the schedules during the 18 months following the Bill's coming in to force.
I may also draw your attention to a provision in the Bill that would extend the prohibition on importing pornographic material or hate literature, as it appears in the present Customs Tariff, beyond the expiry date of December 31, 1987.
Mr. Speaker, as you no doubt recall, this provision, which appears in Schedule C of the present Customs Tariff, was last amended in 1986. The expiry date was to apply to this provision since it was expected that amendments to the provisions in the Criminal Code dealing with pornography would have become effective by that date. Hon. Members are of course aware that the legislation provides a more specific definition of pornography and that these definitions, as soon as they have been approved by Parliament, will be included in the Customs Tariff. Since amendments to the Criminal Code are subject to scrutiny by the House, the Government has preferred to extend the application of this provision for an additional period of six months to ensure effective control of imports of this kind of material.
There is another point I would like to mention. The revised legislation maintains the present tariff treatment for books and other publications. Hon. Members will notice that books and other publications are generally taxed at a rate of 10 per cent. Mr. Speaker, I may explain that despite this statutory rate, books will continue to enter duty free by order of remission. We found it necessary to maintain the 10 per cent duty because of the multilateral trade negotiations now proceeding in Geneva. The Government would consider reducing these tariffs in the course of these negotiations, in exchange for concessions by our trading partners.
The Harmonized System will bring about a fundamental change in the way goods are described for customs purposes. Under the new system, there will inevitably be a number of changes regarding the rate of duty applied to certain goods. However, we have tried to keep the impact on Canadian importers and producers to a minimum. Generally speaking, the conversion will have no impact on revenue.
I should like to deal now with the question of timing. Hon. Members are fully aware that the date set for implementing the harmonized system-January 1, 1988-is getting ever closer. This is why we will have to proceed with dispatch in our consideration of this Bill so that Canada be in a position to honour its commitments to its international partners. Hopefully Hon. Members will give due priority to the study and speedy adoption of this measure.
October 29, 1987

The Government acted as quickly as possible to be sure it would be able to have the legislation passed before January 1, 1988. Canada's trade sector, particularly importers and exporters, look forward to seeing this legislative measure in the statute books. Similarly our main trade partners who will also be switching to tariff systems based on the harmonized system next January 1 expect Canada to play its role in international development.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that Bill C-87 is an important initiative on the part of the Government. It has the support of importers and businessmen who made a number of representations to pave the way for implementation on New Year's Day 1988. It deserves the full consideration of Hon. Members. After examination I am sure they will agree that this Bill will bring significant improvement to Canada's tariff statutes. Given the benefits which businessmen and Canadian industries stand to gain under the new system, I hope all Hon. Members will readily support the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, the Ways and Means motion in this particular case looks remarkably intimidating and runs to two big volumes. However, the principle of this Bill is quite simple. It is one of harmonizing the descriptions of commodities and the coding system that are now used for tariffs. This is the first fundamental revision since Confederation.
Our present system is quite complex because goods are slotted into one of 12 groups according to end use. Therefore goods will often fall into more than one category which can cause confusion.
The decision to harmonize and to standardize so that the major industrial countries would be using approximately the same system was undertaken on a multilateral basis with the European Economic Community, the United States and Japan. In Canada work on this has been going on since 1981, although the international negotiations only began in October, 1986.
The Bill before us will increase the number of tariff items from 3,500 to 8,000, and that is simply the subdivision of items. Naturally, we all know that as a result of Canada's negotiations through the years with GATT more and more of our trade is free of tariff.
Also as a result of increasing the number of categories, this Bill will increase the accuracy of trade data. It should be easier for both importers and exporters to classify their goods, therefore, business should be free of the need to have classification appeals which are time consuming and expensive for industry, and also for government, because they eat up a lot of taxpayers' dollars.
The detailed categories should be easier to use. Also, there should be advantages, from the point of trading, because our
Customs Tariff
major trading partners will be using the same classification system for tariffs. This does not necessarily mean that in each case the tariffs will be the same. In theory, this Bill before us is revenue neutral. That is one of the things that remains to be seen.
We are usually told when this type of Bill appears in the House that it is simple, it is technical, and no one disagrees on the principle and, therefore, we should be able to pass it quickly. We have all found through experience that a Bill which appears simple to officials and bureaucrats often has hidden costs and complexities; hidden that is from bureaucrats but very obvious to the business people using the Bill.
Although I do not feel that we need an extensive debate at second reading on this Bill, I would certainly suggest that it go to a legislative committee which would call witnesses. The witnesses who should be heard from would include the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, representatives of importers and exporters, and representatives of small business. Before we put this Bill in place we should know exactly what is involved in terms of costs and convenience for the users of this new system. We should be assured that they are satisfied that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.
While the Minister has stated that the new legislation will be of significant benefit to Canadian importers, manufacturers, and producers, and that it will result in a more transparent "user friendly" tariff system, we should also know of any possible complications on the other side.
One fairly clear advantage of this new system, and of having it co-ordinated with systems of our major trading partners, is that for the first time statistical trade data will be compatible with the tariff. That should both improve Canada's trade statistics or the quality of reporting, and it should also make it easier to reconcile and compare trade statistics as between Canada and other countries.
Of course, having more accurate import and export data is an advantage in international trade negotiations such as the Uruguay Round of multilateral trade negotiations in which Canada is a participant. It has also been said that the new system is more compatible with modern automated customs processing procedures, and that it will form a fundamental part of National Revenue's new customs commercial system to be implemented on January 1, 1988.
Members in the House regularly receive complaints from importers about delays in getting their goods through customs. If this particular reform is part of anything that assists and speeds up that process, it would be a distinct advantage.
I stated at the outset that this is the first fundamental revision of our commodity description system since Confederation. As the Government is modernizing that system, it has also taken the opportunity to include in this Bill some updating of the legislative provisions to the customs tariff, some of which contain wording from the last century.

October 29, 1987
Another change in the Bill is the incorporation of the Duties Relief Act into the customs tariff, so that we now have brought together in one statute all the legislative provisions relating to the conditions under which customs duties on imported goods are either imposed or relieved.
We have been told that officials have consulted extensively on this Bill with trade associations, customs brokers, and interested parties. But I would repeat, no matter how extensive those consultations have been, they are no substitute for a committee of the House receiving witnesses, holding public hearings, and being quite sure that all the implications have been fully taken into consideration.
The Minister has stated that this was designed to be revenue neutral over-all, but within that some individual rates of duty will be increased or decreased. Before giving this Bill third and final reading, Members of Parliament should be very clear about the exact financial implications, and which sectors will be impacted by these increases and decreases.
This Bill does retain special preferences for the Commonwealth Caribbean countries. It should also be carefully reviewed in committee to ensure that the provisions for developing countries match those in the general preferential tariff.
There is another exception in that the Government has retained the current 10 per cent statutory rate of duty on books and related publications. This is an item on which many of us in the House disagree. But by virtue of a remission order, in fact the goods are entering Canada on a duty-free basis. We may wish to consider whether it is satisfactory having one thing in the statute, and a remission order to negative it, and whether it is not time to change the statute.
In his press release the Minister stated, that,-"given the magnitude of the tariff conversion that has taken place, some 'fine-tuning' may be required for a limited period following implementation on January 1, 1988". I would suggest that if we have good enough committee hearings, perhaps some of the necessary changes could be made now before the Bill comes into effect.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on Monday, October 26, the Government defeated every opposition amendment which attempted to correct ambiguities and gaps in the Meech Lake Accord.
In particular, the Government refused amendments which would have protected the Charter of Rights from any possible impact by the Accord. I personally do not believe that the Meech Lake Accord impacts adversely on the Charter, but others do, and there is legal uncertainty as a result.
